content: Anaphylaxis is a severe, acute systemic allergic reaction that can be life-threatening. H1-antihistamines are frequently used as an additional therapy in the management of anaphylaxis. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the potential benefits and harms of H1-antihistamines in treating anaphylaxis. In the previous version of this review, the search for relevant studies was conducted up to June 2006. For this updated version, the search was extended to include databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL, The Cochrane Library 2010, Issue 11), MEDLINE (1966 to November 2010), EMBASE (1966 to November 2010), CINAHL (1982 to November 2010), and ISI Web of Science (1945 to November 2010). Additionally, pharmaceutical companies and international experts in the field of anaphylaxis were contacted to identify any unpublished data. The inclusion criteria for this review required randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared the use of H1-antihistamines with either a placebo or no intervention. Two independent authors reviewed the articles to determine their eligibility for inclusion in the analysis. However, no studies meeting the inclusion criteria were identified during the review process. As a result, the authors were unable to provide any evidence-based recommendations for the clinical use of H1-antihistamines in the treatment of anaphylaxis. The authors concluded that randomized controlled trials are necessary to address this gap in knowledge, although designing and conducting such studies may present significant challenges.
